Abstract
Background
Drug discovery is known for the large amount of money and time it consumes and the high risk it takes. Drug repositioning has, therefore, become a popular approach to save time and cost by finding novel indications for approved drugs. In order to distinguish these novel indications accurately in a great many of latent associations between drugs and diseases, it is necessary to exploit abundant heterogeneous information about drugs and diseases.

Results
In this article, we propose a meta-path-based computational method called NEDD to predict novel associations between drugs and diseases using heterogeneous information. First, we construct a heterogeneous network as an undirected graph by integrating drug-drug similarity, disease-disease similarity, and known drug-disease associations. NEDD uses meta paths of different lengths to explicitly capture the indirect relationships, or high order proximity, within drugs and diseases, by which the low dimensional representation vectors of drugs and diseases are obtained. NEDD then uses a random forest classifier to predict novel associations between drugs and diseases.

Conclusions
The experiments on a gold standard dataset which contains 1933 validated drug–disease associations show that NEDD produces superior prediction results compared with the state-of-the-art approaches.

result.paraphrase:
Abstract

Background
Drug discovery is known to be expensive, time-consuming, and highly risky. As a result, drug repositioning has become a widely used strategy for saving time and cost by identifying new indications for approved drugs. To accurately distinguish these new indications among the many latent associations between drugs and diseases, abundant heterogeneous information about both drugs and diseases must be leveraged.

Results
In this article, we present a meta-path-based computational approach called NEDD for predicting novel drug–disease associations using heterogeneous information. We first build a heterogeneous network as an undirected graph by combining drug–drug similarity, disease–disease similarity, and known drug–disease associations. NEDD employs meta paths of varying lengths to explicitly capture indirect relationships, or high-order proximity, among drugs and diseases, from which low-dimensional representation vectors for drugs and diseases are derived. It then applies a random forest classifier to predict new drug–disease associations.

Conclusions
Experiments on a gold-standard dataset containing 1,933 validated drug–disease associations demonstrate that NEDD delivers superior prediction performance compared with state-of-the-art methods.
